parts.title: From Solid Balls to Plum Pudding

lines.text: This pencil tip is made of carbon.
Cut it smaller and smaller, down to single carbon atoms.
“Atom” comes from the Greek word “atomos.” It means “can't be cut.”
lines.tts: Atom comes from the Greek word, [[ˈætəmɑːs.]] It means, can't be cut.

lines.text: About 2,400 years ago, Leucippus and his student Democritus had an idea.
lines.tts: About twenty-four hundred years ago, [[luːsˈɪpəs]] and his student [[dɪmˈɑːkɹɪɾəs]] had an idea.

lines.text: Everything is made of atoms and empty space.
Aristotle disagreed.
He said everything is fire, air, earth, and water.
Most people believed him for almost 2,000 years.
lines.tts: Most people believed him for almost two thousand years.

lines.text: How can we learn what's inside something too small to see?
We do experiments: tests that check an idea.
By 1800, chemists knew two laws: rules nature always follows.
lines.tts: By eighteen hundred, chemists knew two laws: rules nature always follows.

lines.text: First, Antoine Lavoisier. When chemicals react in a sealed jar, mass stays the same.
lines.tts: First, [[ɑːntwˈɑːn lɑːvwɑːzɪˈeɪ.]] When chemicals react in a sealed jar, mass stays the same.

lines.text: Mass is how much stuff there is.
Second, Joseph Proust. Water always has 8 grams of oxygen per gram of hydrogen.
lines.tts: Second, Joseph Proost. Water always has eight grams of oxygen per gram of hydrogen.

lines.text: In 1803, John Dalton explained both laws.
lines.tts: In eighteen oh three, John Dalton explained both laws.

lines.text: Atoms are tiny solid balls that can't be split.
All atoms of one element, or pure substance, are alike.
Atoms join in whole numbers, never half an atom.
This is the Solid Sphere model: a picture that explains the clues.
It predicts that there's nothing inside an atom.
In 1897, J. J. Thomson tested a cathode ray tube.
lines.tts: In eighteen ninety-seven, Jay Jay Thomson tested a cathode ray tube.

lines.text: It's a glass tube with most of the air pumped out.
A glowing beam shoots from the negative end, called the cathode,
to the positive end, called the anode.
An object in the beam casts a sharp shadow.
So the beam travels in straight lines.
The beam bends toward a positive plate.
Charge comes in plus and minus. Opposites pull together.
So the beam is made of tiny negative bits, called particles.
A magnet bends the beam too.
Thomson changed the metal, and the beam stayed the same.
So these particles are in every kind of atom.
And they're over 1,000 times lighter than a hydrogen atom.
lines.tts: And they're over one thousand times lighter than a hydrogen atom.

lines.text: He had discovered the electron.
Prediction: nothing inside. Result: smaller parts inside!
So the Solid Sphere model gets updated.
Whole atoms have no overall charge.
So something positive must balance the electrons.
In 1904, Thomson made the Plum Pudding model.
lines.tts: In nineteen oh four, Thomson made the Plum Pudding model.

lines.text: Electrons sit in a ball of spread-out positive charge.
Like blueberries in a muffin.
Plum pudding is an old British dessert.
Next time, a gold foil experiment puts this model to the test.

parts.title: From Gold Foil to the Quantum Model

lines.text: Last time, the atom went from a solid ball to plum pudding.
Next, Ernest Rutherford's team tested the Plum Pudding model.
Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at gold foil.
lines.tts: Hans [[ɡˈaɪɡɚ]] and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at gold foil.

lines.text: Alpha particles are fast, heavy, and positive.
They shoot out of radioactive material on their own.
The gold foil was much thinner than paper.
A screen around it flashed wherever a particle hit.
They counted the flashes in a dark room, using a microscope.
Prediction: the positive charge is spread thin.
So every particle should zip straight through.
Here's what really happened.
Most particles went straight through.
A few bent at big angles.
And about 1 in 8,000 bounced almost straight back!
lines.tts: And about one in eight thousand bounced almost straight back!

lines.text: Rutherford said it was like firing a giant shell at tissue paper,
and having it bounce back and hit you!
So the atom is mostly empty space.
In the middle is a tiny, positive center called the nucleus.
It holds almost all the mass. Electrons are outside it.
Make the nucleus a baseball, and the atom is 5 miles wide.
lines.tts: Make the nucleus a baseball, and the atom is five miles wide.

lines.text: Plum Pudding is updated. This is the Nuclear Model.
Later, in 1932, came one more piece.
lines.tts: Later, in nineteen thirty-two, came one more piece.

lines.text: Hydrogen has 1 proton, a positive particle in the nucleus.
lines.tts: Hydrogen has one proton, a positive particle in the nucleus.

lines.text: Helium has 2 protons, but 4 times the mass.
lines.tts: Helium has two protons, but four times the mass.

lines.text: James Chadwick found the missing mass: neutrons, with no charge.
But where exactly are the electrons?
Physics said circling electrons should spiral into the nucleus.
The clue came from light.
Hydrogen gas glows when electricity runs through it.
A prism, a wedge of glass, splits that light into colors.
White light makes a full rainbow.
But hydrogen makes only four thin lines.
Every element has its own lines, like a fingerprint.
That's why metals make different colored flames.
In 1913, Niels Bohr explained the lines.
lines.tts: In nineteen thirteen, Niels Bohr explained the lines.

lines.text: Electrons can only be on certain levels, each with a fixed energy.
It's like stairs. You stand on a step, never between.
Add energy, and an electron jumps up a level.
When it falls back, it gives off one exact color.
A small drop, from level 3 to 2, gives red.
lines.tts: A small drop, from level three to two, gives red.

lines.text: A bigger drop, from 5 to 2, gives violet: more energy.
lines.tts: A bigger drop, from five to two, gives violet: more energy.

lines.text: Nuclear is updated. This is the Planetary Model: electrons on rings.
Bohr's model matched hydrogen perfectly.
But it failed for atoms with more electrons, even helium.
In 1924, Louis de Broglie said electrons also act like waves.
lines.tts: In nineteen twenty-four, Louis [[də bɹˈɔɪ]] said electrons also act like waves.

lines.text: In 1926, Erwin Schrödinger wrote an equation treating electrons as waves.
lines.tts: In nineteen twenty-six, Erwin Shrohdinger wrote an equation treating electrons as waves.

lines.text: Its answers are orbitals: places an electron is likely to be.
In 1927, Werner Heisenberg showed we can't know an electron's exact path.
lines.tts: In nineteen twenty-seven, Werner Heisenberg showed we can't know an electron's exact path.

lines.text: Imagine 1,000 snapshots of where the electron is.
lines.tts: Imagine one thousand snapshots of where the electron is.

lines.text: Stack them up, and you get a fuzzy cloud.
It's thickest where the electron is most likely to be.
Planetary is updated. This is the Quantum Model.
Fun fact: J. J. Thomson won a Nobel Prize for the electron particle.
lines.tts: Fun fact: Jay Jay Thomson won a Nobel Prize for the electron particle.

lines.text: In 1927, his son, G. P. Thomson, showed electrons act like waves.
lines.tts: In nineteen twenty-seven, his son, Gee Pee Thomson, showed electrons act like waves.

lines.text: The son shared a Nobel Prize for it!
Five models. Each one changed because of evidence.
Two laws. Cathode rays. Gold foil. Light lines. Electron waves.
Each model made a prediction. An experiment tested it.
When the result didn't fit, scientists updated the model.
Each experiment didn't throw science away.
It made our picture of the atom better.
